files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Authoring.BaseCharacterLocomotorAuthoring<TProfile>.BaseCharacterLocomotorBaker<TAuthoring, TStateMachine, TStates, TContext, TInput, TStateData>
files.Summary:
Baker for the CharacterAuthoring. Converts the authoring data into an ECS entity with the following setup:

  1. Creates the character entity with TransformUsageFlags.ManualOverride and manually adds LocalTransform and LocalToWorld built from the authoring Transform. The character is always produced as an unparented root entity — related entities (player, follower/model) link to it via explicit references, not via the ECS transform hierarchy or LinkedEntityGroup.
  2. If a CharacterProfile is provided: – Generates or reuses a BlobAssetReference from the profile asset (and calls DependsOn so changes re-bake automatically) – Adds LocomotionInput to drive character movement from player input or AI Agent – Builds a CapsuleCollider from profile settings (CapsuleGeometry + CollisionFilter) and adds it as a PhysicsCollider blob asset – Registers the character with the physics world (PhysicsWorldIndex) – Adds LocomotionProfileBlob (points to the blob asset), LocomotionVelocity, LocomotionContact, and LocomotionGravity (seeded from the default physics-step gravity) – Adds the state machine component left at its default state (enum value 0); no explicit initial state is assigned during baking

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Authoring.BaseCharacterLocomotorAuthoring<TProfile>
files.Summary:
Serves as a base class for authoring character entities with locomotion capabilities. Designed to work with a profile of type TProfile, enabling customization of character movement and behavior through specific profile definitions. Contains shared properties and functionality for setting up entities related to character locomotion, including rendering models and defining state machines through further specialization. The class includes a nested abstract baker class used for converting authoring data into ECS entities with the following configurations:

  1. Associates the authored character with a profile asset (defining locomotion behavior and rules).
  2. Supports optional assignment of a prefab model entity for visual representation.
  3. Facilitates the integration of locomotion state machines, states, and custom contexts specific to the movement profile.

files.Summary: Struct for collecting the closest collider cast hits while ignoring a specific entity. Implements the ICollector interface to gather and manage collider cast hit results. Filters out results that do not meet defined criteria such as hits associated with an ignored entity or backface collisions. This is particularly useful in physics-related computations where certain entities need to be excluded, such as in character or object traversal and detection systems.

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Runtime.Physics.ClosestDistanceHitCollectorIgnoreSelf

Implements the ICollector interface to manage distance hit results and filters hits based on custom criteria such as excluding hits involving a specified entity or backface collisions. Useful in scenarios where distance queries need to selectively exclude certain entities or object surfaces, e.g., during character or object navigation systems in physics simulations.

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Runtime.Physics.ClosestRaycastHitCollectorIgnoreSelf
files.Summary: Struct for collecting closest raycast hits while ignoring a specified entity. Implements the ICollector interface to manage raycast hit results and avoids processing hits that do not meet the criteria, such as hits associated with a self entity or backface collisions. Useful in scenarios where certain entities need to be ignored during raycasting computations, such as character locomotion systems in physics-based simulations.

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Runtime.Physics.LocomotionHitFilter

The policy is split into a world-independent part (decidable from the hit fields alone) and a world-dependent part (requires the body table), so the world-independent rules can be verified without a PhysicsWorld and the three collectors stop duplicating the same checks.

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Tests.Editor.Defects.CameraRigFollowUnloadDefectTests
files.Summary:
Reproduction of defect ticket camera-rig-follow-unload-defect (Plan~/defects/camera-rig-follow-unload-defect.md), executed by qa on 2026-08-01. The ticket's "Reproduction" section names this fixture as its canonical reproduction; this header is the other half of that link. Do not delete either without the other.

What the ticket claims, and what these tests execute (its numbered steps 1-5): a player entity carrying is bound to a camera rig by PlayerGoManagerSystem (InitializationSystemGroup); destroying that entity later in the SAME frame — from a system inside SimulationSystemGroup, the ordinary gameplay path — leaves it in the camera registry when ApplyCameraTransformJob is scheduled over it in TransformSystemGroup, and the job's unguarded LocalToWorldLookup[PlayerEntities[index]] throws.

CONVENTION — a defect test that currently REPRODUCES carries [Category("KnownDefect")] and [Explicit]. Explicit keeps it out of an unfiltered suite run (the test framework reports it as skipped, and the studio gate counts only failed + inconclusive), so a known, ticketed defect does not red the gate, while the test itself stays in the repository as non-regression data. Run it on demand by naming it: -testFilter "*CameraRigFollowUnloadDefectTests*" — a named filter is an explicit match. When the defect is fixed, DELETE the two attributes: the assertions are written against the CORRECT behaviour the ticket's "Fixed when" states, never against the bug, so a fix turns them green with no rewrite. The tests below without those attributes already pass today and are the anti-vacuity pairs — they are guard-rails on any future fix (a fix that drains the whole registry, or that unbinds a live player, breaks them).

Cheapest useful level: EditMode, one real world, the package's own systems in their real groups. No baked SubScene and no play mode — the defect is an ordering hole between two system groups and a missing predicate, both of which a plain world update reproduces.

Fixture constraints, stated because they shape what this suite can claim: (1) EDIT MODE NEVER RUNS Awake. PlayerGoAuthoring.Awake is what creates the CameraTarget child in a running game, so this fixture wires CameraTarget by hand; the shape handed to PlayerGoManagerSystem is identical either way. (2) EDIT MODE CANNOT Object.Destroy. The frame AFTER the destroy, PlayerGoManagerSystem's cleanup loop calls Object.Destroy on the player GameObject, which is a play-mode API; from edit mode it errors. That error is an artifact of the harness, not of the defect, so the console gate below is scoped to entries attributable to the CAMERA path () rather than to every console error — the same scoping choice the 0.8.1 hybrid fixture made for the same reason.

files.Summary:
Reproduction of defect ticket hybrid-registry-hygiene (Plan~/defects/hybrid-registry-hygiene.md), executed by qa on 2026-08-01. The ticket's "Reproduction" section names this fixture as its canonical reproduction; this header is the other half of that link. Do not delete either without the other.

What the ticket claims, and what these tests execute (its numbered steps 1-6): the hybrid transform registry lives in static fields of EntityGoTransformSyncSystem reached through a static Instance copy, so every World in the process registers into the same two collections while Entity ids are only meaningful in the world that issued them. Two live worlds therefore share one registry, each world's prune walks the other's entries, and either world's teardown disposes the collections for both.

THIS FIXTURE DELIBERATELY VIOLATES the 0.8.1 "one world at a time" fixture constraint (Plan~/stories/unload-sync-contract.md §5). That constraint exists BECAUSE of the defect reproduced here, so violating it is the point — it is not carelessness, and it is why this suite does not derive from BehaviorTestsFixture (which owns exactly one world).

CONVENTION — a defect test that currently REPRODUCES carries [Category("KnownDefect")] and [Explicit]. Explicit keeps it out of an unfiltered suite run (the framework reports it as skipped, and the studio gate counts only failed + inconclusive), so a known, ticketed defect does not red the gate while the test stays in the repository as non-regression data. Run it on demand by naming it: -testFilter "*HybridRegistryHygieneDefectTests*". When the defect is fixed, DELETE the two attributes: every assertion is written against the CORRECT behaviour the ticket's "Fixed when" states — a companion follows its own world's entity, and is unaffected by another world's update or teardown — never against the bug, so a fix turns them green with no rewrite.

Assertions are behavioural (does this world's companion still follow its own entity?) rather than counts read off the internal static seam, deliberately: the seam is itself part of what a per-world design would have to change, so a count assertion could not survive a fix. The seam is read only for OBSERVATIONS quoted in failure messages, through (which falls back to reflection and returns 0 rather than throwing if the members move).

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Tests.Editor.JumpOffMomentumTests
files.Summary:
PLT-7b — jump-off momentum on a dedicated, isolated Gym surface.

Behaviour under test (from PLT-7b): a character riding a horizontally moving platform carries the platform's horizontal velocity into a jump. At the instant it leaves the surface its horizontal speed equals the platform's. Platform momentum is inherited automatically by the controller (Jumping.OnEnterState does HorizontalVelocity += PlatformHorizontalVelocity, exactly once); a game's jump logic must not add it a second time. If it were double-added the lift-off horizontal speed would be ~2x the platform speed — which this test rejects.

============================================================================================ SCENE CONTRACT for dev (plt7-author-scene) — subscene filename: "Jump_MovingPlatform"

Resolution is by exact filename (see BehaviorTestsFixture.ResolveSceneGuid); the folder is dev's choice — recommended: Samples/BehaviorShowCase/Scenes/BehaviourTests/KinematicPlatform/Jump_MovingPlatform.unity (sibling of the KinematicPlatform scenes; shares the Jump_ prefix of Jump_FlatGround / Jump_OneWayPlatforms since the behaviour is a jump). This test is RED until that scene exists (ResolveSceneGuid fails loudly when the SceneAsset is absent).

The scene must contain, isolated (one character, one platform), and self-contained:

  1. One KINEMATIC platform authored with MovingPlatformAuthoring (+ PlatformAuthoring + kinematic Rigidbody). Its Track is two waypoints laid out along +X so the platform translates in a straight line at a constant horizontal velocity through the whole run (make the leg long enough — e.g. 20 m — that it never reaches the far waypoint and reverses before lift-off). Authored Speed = 1 (m/s) — the MovingPlatformAuthoring default, matching the existing KinematicPlatform scenes (which author 1 / 10 / 100). Direction = world +X. => the character must inherit a horizontal velocity of ~(+1, 0) in the XZ plane at lift-off.
  2. One character bot (the SimpleCharacter prefab used by the other BehaviourTests scenes) resting on top of the platform, with SimpleCharacterBotAuthoring Move = (0,0,0) and Jump = true. Zero movement means the ONLY horizontal velocity the character can have at lift-off is what it inherits from the platform. The one-shot jump waits until the character is grounded (FromIdlingToJumping requires IsGroundingContact), so the bot settles onto and rides the moving platform before jumping — no ramp needed.
  3. Default -Y gravity, character upright (so "horizontal" == the XZ plane).

If the scene depends on shared physics/ground config it may reuse World-SubScene (loaded in SetUp below); the character rides the elevated platform, so a shared floor does not interfere.

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Tests.Editor.UnloadSync.HybridCompanionFixture
files.Summary:
The streaming substrate for the hybrid unload-sync epic: a world carrying the hybrid systems, characters bound to live companion GameObjects through the package's own registration path, and a console recorder so "no sync error" is a named assertion.

No baked SubScene. The contract established (§1.2, §5 fixture constraint 3) that an entity-scene unload IS EntityManager.DestroyEntity(query), and that single-entity and query destroys share one code path — so EntityManager.DestroyEntity(Entity) on a companion entity reproduces the IDENTICAL entity state an unload leaves: a cleanup-residue entity that still exists, still carries , and no longer carries LocalToWorld. Every destroy in this suite asserts that residue shape before pumping, so the fixture cannot silently stop reproducing the real thing.

Binding uses the real path end to end: an entity carrying is picked up by EntityGoInitialisationSystem, which instantiates the companion, adds and calls AssignEntity → RegisterTransform. The test never registers anything itself.

Two deliberate fixture choices, both recorded because they shape what the suite can claim:

(1) EntityGoCleanupSystem is DISABLED. It tears the companion down with Object.Destroy, which is a play-mode API — calling it from edit mode logs an error of its own and would drown the very console assertion this epic is about. Disabling it holds the window the contract identifies as the defect's home open for as long as a test needs: entity dead, companion still alive and still registered. That window is one frame in the shipped samples and Delay seconds for a consumer using a DestructionManager; the sync system's behaviour inside it is identical either way, and it is the only thing under test here. HUS-4 (the companions leave with their scene) is that system's clause, is unchanged by this epic (contract §9 A3), and is not asserted here.

(2) Each test calls as its first statement. The framework's implicit "an error was logged, so the test fails" would make every assertion in this suite fail with the same anonymous message, including the registry-invariant tests that must fail on the REGISTRY and not on the console. The console gate is instead asserted explicitly by , which names the clause and prints the offending entries.

Anti-vacuity: and are the paired positives. An implementation that "fixes" the leak by clearing the whole registry, or by removing an entity without its transform, passes INV-R2 and INV-R4 and fails those two.

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Tests.Editor.UnloadSync.HybridUnloadSyncTests
files.Summary:
What a consumer streaming entity scenes observes — HUS-1, HUS-2, HUS-3, HUS-6, HUS-8, HUS-10 of [unload-sync-spec]. These tests assert the CONSUMER-VISIBLE surface: models on screen (companion transforms) and entries in the console. The registry property that a symptom-only fix would leave broken is asserted separately, in .

Anti-vacuity: every "nothing was thrown" assertion is paired with a positive that a frozen or no-op sync path fails — a character is MOVED and its companion must arrive at the new position in the same frame. A fix that silences the exception by never scheduling the job at all would turn , and red.

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Tests.Editor.UnloadSync.SyncErrorRecorder
files.Summary:
Captures everything a consumer would see in the console while a world is pumped, so that HUS-2 / HUS-3 ("the console records no sync error — zero, not fewer than before") can be asserted as a named gate instead of relying on the test framework's implicit unexpected-log failure.

Why a recorder rather than LogAssert.NoUnexpectedReceived() alone: the defect surfaces from inside a Burst-compiled IJobParallelForTransform. A job exception is caught at the job boundary and logged — possibly from a worker thread — so the capture must be threaded (Application.logMessageReceivedThreaded), and it may alternatively be re-thrown on the main thread when the dependency is completed. Both routes are folded into one list here ( covers the throw route), so a single assertion covers the symptom however the runtime chooses to surface it, and the failure message carries the exception text that identifies it as the reported defect.

Attribution: applies the spec's glossary definition of a "sync error" — an entry the console attributes to the package's hybrid transform sync. It is used to annotate the failure message; the gate itself asserts on every recorded error, which is the stricter reading and is only sustainable because the fixture's positive-control test proves the pumped world is otherwise quiet.

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Tests.Performance.FrameBudgetTestBase
files.Summary:
PERF-4 (Mode B — architecture §3.2.2) shared body for the 30 000-character frame-budget gates that back (or refute) the "30 000 characters @ 60 fps" store claim (DOC-2). PERF-4 is split into two honest variants that share this base and differ ONLY in whether rendering is folded into the measured frame time:

  • PERF-4a — simulation (): runs headless (-nographics, forge default), so Measure.Frames times the CPU simulation loop with rendering EXCLUDED. This is the sub-claim number.
  • PERF-4b — full loop (): runs with a real graphics device (-force-d3d11, via forge test … --graphics) and a runtime camera framing the population, so the measured frame time INCLUDES render + present. This is the number a customer reads as "30 000 @ 60 fps".

Each variant SELF-GATES on the graphics device ( vs SystemInfo.graphicsDeviceType) and Assert.Ignore(string)s when the run is in the wrong mode — so one forge test --platform playmode asserts the sim number while the render test ignores, and one forge test --platform playmode --graphics asserts the render number while the sim test ignores. Neither variant is a real IL2CPP player build; even the -force-d3d11 offscreen render is closer-but-not-equal to a standalone Player (the truest number is a shipped build).

Grounded AND moving precondition (director directive 2026-07-17). Before measuring, this base waits until the spawned population is at STEADY STATE: every character is grounded () AND at least of them are moving (planar speed > ). Movement is BAKED into the BotCharacterPerf prefab (SimpleCharacterBotAuthoring.Move, seeded onto at bake time and carried through the spawner's Instantiate by the IncludePrefab query in SimpleCharacterBotBakingSystem), so the spawned population self-locomotes from the first tick with no runtime input write — the number reflects the real working scenario (active locomotion + physics + render), not an idle/settling transient. A failure to reach steady state inside the timeout fails loudly, so a stale/idle measurement can never be recorded.

Claim linkage / clean-room canon (ADR-4). The median-≤-16.67 ms assertion is made ONLY on the clean-room reference machine (, or forced via the env var). On every OTHER machine the test still runs the full workload and logs the number, but replaces the assertion with an explicit Assert.Ignore(string). A breach on the reference machine REMOVES/relabels the marketing claim (DOC-2 re-spec, new PR) and never blocks the merge — PERF-4 gates the claim, not the merge.

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Tests.Performance.PerfSpawnerFixture
files.Summary:
Shared plumbing for the PERF-1…5 perf harness over the PerfSpawner surface (Samples/BehaviorShowCase/Scenes/PerfTests/PerfSpawner.unity). Loads the scene as a subscene, drives the non-interactive spawn seam, and ticks the world deterministically until the spawned population settles grounded.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── SEAM CONTRACT for dev (implement EXACTLY this — shape from architecture §3.2.3 item 1): ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. New public component in the SHOWCASE spawner assembly (WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Tests.Runtime, file under Samples/BehaviorShowCase/Runtime/):

    namespace WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Tests.Runtime
{
    public struct SpawnRequest : IComponentData { public int Count; }
}

  2. Consumption in SpawningSystem (InitializationSystemGroup, inside m_world.Update()): when a SpawnRequest exists, spawn EXACTLY Count characters of the spawner prefab in the deterministic Grid layout (ADR-5: Grid is the locked perf pattern), then CONSUME the request (remove the component / destroy the request entity) so it fires once. Grid derivation from N (per §3.3): columns = ceil(sqrt(Count)); rows = ceil(Count / columns); spawn exactly Count entities (last row partial — NOT columns*rows rounded up), using the AUTHORED GridSpacing, centered on the spawner origin (LocalToWorld.Position). The interactive Enter-key path and this seam MUST share ONE spawn implementation (redraw the boundary so the spawn trigger is not welded to input).

  3. Headless input guard (blocks this fixture TODAY): SpawningSystem.OnUpdate dereferences Keyboard.current/Mouse.current unconditionally. In batchmode / a headless test world these are null, so the very first world Update (during LoadSubScenes) NREs before the seam is ever reached. Guard every Keyboard.current/Mouse.current access with a null check.

The SpawnRequest seam (items 1–3 above) is now IMPLEMENTED, so this assembly compiles and the fast N=100 correctness case is green. The remaining Red lives in the behaviour, not the compile: the 30 000-capacity case (PERF-1) and the per-tier zero-alloc gate (PERF-5) are the signals that fail if the sim can't scale or allocates on the tick.

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Tests.Performance.RenderFrameBudgetTests
files.Summary:
PERF-4b — the 30 000-character FULL-LOOP frame budget (rendering INCLUDED). Runs with a real graphics device under -force-d3d11 (run with forge test --platform playmode --graphics) and creates a runtime camera + light framing the population, so Measure.Frames times the full player loop: simulation PLUS the character render path PLUS present. This is the number a customer reads as "30 000 @ 60 fps" — it is the one PERF-4 must be adjudicated on. The BotCharacterPerf render path is Entity Graphics: a baked MeshRenderer becomes RenderMeshArray + MaterialMeshInfo drawn by the pure-ECS instanced batch renderer (no per-character companion GameObject), so the render cost at 30k is the EG cull/batch/submit + present cost; that is the honest point.

Self-gates via = true: under the headless -nographics default this test Assert.Ignores (a headless run cannot measure render), so run it explicitly with --graphics. Even -force-d3d11 offscreen render is closer-but-not-equal to a real IL2CPP Player build — the truest number is a standalone build. The median-≤-16.67 ms assertion is made on the clean-room reference machine only (ADR-4).

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Tests.Performance.SimulationFrameBudgetTests
files.Summary:
PERF-4a — the 30 000-character SIMULATION frame budget (rendering EXCLUDED). Runs headless under -nographics (the forge default; run with forge test --platform playmode), so Measure.Frames times the CPU simulation loop only — no GPU, no present. This is the honest simulation sub-claim: what the character-controller sim costs per frame at 30k, NOT a rendered fps. For the full-loop number a customer reads as "30 000 @ 60 fps", see (PERF-4b, --graphics).

Self-gates via = false: if a real graphics device is present (a --graphics run) this test Assert.Ignores so render work is never folded into the sim number. The full workload (spawn 30k, grounded+moving steady state, measure) still runs; the median-≤-16.67 ms assertion is made on the clean-room reference machine only (ADR-4).

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Tests.Performance.SimulationFrequencyMatrixTests
files.Summary:
Sim-rate × population cost matrix (EditMode, characterization — NOT a gate). Sweeps the character count {1, 100, 1000, 10000, 20000, 30000} against the simulation frequency {20, 30, 50, 60} Hz and records, for each cell, the cost of ONE 60-fps-cadence simulation-path frame at that rate and population. It answers "how does the per-frame simulation cost scale with sim frequency and crowd size?" — the question behind the 30 000 @ 60 fps claim once the sim runs at a real 60 Hz.

Metric per cell — sim-path ms per 60 fps frame (render EXCLUDED). Each measured frame advances a fixed 1/60 s of world time (the 60-fps render cadence) and runs only the simulation path ( = Initialization + Simulation groups, no presentation/render). At sim rate F the FixedStepSimulationSystemGroup runs F/60 fixed ticks per frame (physics + locomotor over the whole population), so the cell cost rises with F. The figure is directly comparable to the 16.67 ms 60-fps budget (the simulation share of it). Because rendering is not capped in the shipped scenario, a frame rendered faster than 60 fps carries fewer than F/60 ticks and costs less — the 60-fps cadence here is the reference the claim is stated at.

Efficiency: the expensive spawn+settle is paid ONCE per count and reused across all four frequencies (the sim rate is re-applied between measurements via the singleton, which ApplyFixedStepRateSystem pushes onto the group each frame). Mean is the headline (it averages the fixed-tick beat over frames); median is logged alongside. This suite does not assert a budget — it records the surface for the director / DOC-2. The only hard precondition is that the population settles grounded, so a still-falling measurement can never be recorded.

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Tests.Performance.SimulationMemoryTests
files.Summary:
Simulation-path MEMORY ALLOCATION measurement (EditMode). MEASURES ONLY — it does not gate. For each character count {1, 100, 1000, 10000, 20000, 30000} it spawns and settles the population, then measures the managed heap bytes allocated per simulation-path tick (physics + locomotor, presentation excluded) and records it as a SimAllocBytes_{n} sample group in bytes per tick.

Counterpart to (which measures the TIME cost surface): that suite answers "how fast is a frame", this one answers "how much does the sim path allocate". Neither asserts a budget — they are characterization surfaces for the perf report, not pass/fail gates. The one hard precondition here is the same as everywhere in this fixture: the population must settle grounded, so a still-falling measurement can never be recorded.

Method — byte-exact, no instrumentation in the counter span. Allocation is measured with (thread-local, so a background editor task on another thread cannot pollute it) captured AROUND a raw window of sim-path ticks — no Measure.* instrumentation inside the window, whose own per-iteration bookkeeping would otherwise be counted as sim allocation. Two windows are sampled and the larger reported, so a deterministic per-tick allocation (which repeats in both) is never under-reported. A managed allocation on the sim main thread shows up here as a non-zero B/tick figure; a Burst-clean sim path reads 0.

files.Title: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Tests.Performance.SpawnCapacityTests
files.Summary:
PERF-1 correctness precondition: request N via the non-interactive spawn seam, settle, then assert exactly N characters exist, each in ground contact, none below the floor. This is the spawn-count/settle setup that the PERF-2…5 measurements later reuse over the same PerfSpawner surface (architecture §3.2.3, §4 PERF-1 row).

Two tiers are pinned here: the fast N = 100 tier and the capacity-raise N = 30 000 tier (perf-raise-scene-capacity-30k / perf-verify-30k-settles-grounded). Both assert the identical invariant via .
